disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), Combined Presentation, is characterized by developmentally inappropriate and impairing levels of both inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity, with multiple symptoms present for at least six months across two or more settings (e.g., home, school, work). It typically begins in childhood, though it may not be formally recognized until academic or occupational demands exceed the person’s ability to compensate. The course is often chronic, with some symptoms diminishing over time while others persist, leading to functional impairment in organization, time management, and self-regulation. It is distinguished from anxiety, mood, and learning disorders by the pervasive, cross-situational pattern of attentional and behavioral dysregulation that is not better explained by situational stressors or exclusively by other psychiatric or cognitive conditions.

narrative.stressor: Courtney’s difficulties became clinically significant during her first year away from Leechburg, when she enrolled full-time in a competitive data science and design program while also taking on several freelance UX and visualization gigs. The open-ended nature of studio assignments and long-term coding projects, combined with multiple overlapping deadlines, exposed long-standing problems with organizing her work, sequencing tasks, and staying on track once the initial excitement of a project wore off. Over the past year and a half, her pattern of last-minute all-nighters, missed submission windows, and dropped freelance clients began to threaten her academic standing and reputation in the small tech-art community she values, despite strong technical skills and creativity. After a professor suggested that her performance gap and history sounded like more than “poor time management,” and a client formally complained about an unfinished dashboard, she agreed—at her advisor’s urging—to seek a psychiatric evaluation to understand why she could not reliably follow through on work even when highly motivated.
narrative.chief_complaint: I keep starting projects with tons of ideas, but I just can’t seem to follow through and finish my school and freelance work on time.

narrative.stressor: For most of his career, Baha’s energy and quick reactions fit well with the unpredictable tempo of fire service work, and informal coping strategies at the station masked underlying attention and impulse-control problems. About a year and a half ago, as he began taking advanced incident command and leadership courses to prepare for promotion, the job demands shifted toward complex paperwork, prolonged training sessions, and meticulous adherence to evolving protocols, making it harder for him to compensate. Repeated feedback from instructors and his captain about missed details in reports, overlooked steps in training drills, and difficulty staying focused during briefings raised concerns about his readiness for captaincy and, at times, safety on scene. After a near-miss in which he overlooked a key radio update during a multi-engine response, his chief gently suggested a formal evaluation, and Baha—frustrated that his ambition was being undercut by what felt like an inability to stay dialed in—agreed to seek psychiatric help.
narrative.chief_complaint: When I’m in trainings or going over incident plans, my mind drifts and I can’t keep my attention on what’s being said, even though I know it’s important for my job.

narrative.stressor: Miriam had long managed her tendencies toward scattered focus through strict routines and structured consulting work, but her family’s recent relocation to Pahala and her gradual shift out of full-time environmental consulting disrupted the scaffolding she relied on. Over the past 17 months, as she tried to juggle part-time remote projects, community volunteering, and increased family responsibilities in a new cultural and physical environment, she found it increasingly hard to keep track of daily tasks, appointments, and small but important obligations around the home and garden. The contrast between her self-image as a meticulous planner and the growing pile of forgotten errands, missed calls, and rescheduled meetings left her feeling ineffective and confused, especially when her spouse began gently pointing out repeated lapses. After double-booking an important client call and a school meeting for her child—and realizing this pattern had been building since the move—she consulted her primary care provider, who referred her for a psychiatric assessment to explore whether an underlying attention disorder was contributing to her struggles.
narrative.chief_complaint: Lately I keep forgetting everyday things—appointments, calls I need to return, even basic errands—and it’s starting to throw off my home and work routines.
